position.summary: Venezuela entered the week under interim leader Delcy Rodriguez following Maduro's removal, with Maria Corina Machado still in exile and the opposition holding rallies and motorcades demanding her safe return. A Caracas energy summit drew executives from Eni, Repsol, Qatar's UCC, GeoPark, Glencore, and Peabody, signalling foreign capital's renewed interest. The IMF explored establishing a local office. The government publicly acknowledged misuse of the anti-hate law. Venezuela handed an FBI-wanted suspect to Washington. Power outages triggered tire-burning protests in several states, and the 100-day anniversary of twin earthquakes kept housing and compensation demands alive in La Guaira. In Washington, former congressman David Rivera's sentencing and Senate Democrats' challenge to the Pentagon's proposed equity stake in Venezuelan oil turned the energy file into a domestic political fight. Claudia Macero returned from exile. The overall picture was a government projecting openness and deal momentum while retaining firm political control over the pace of transition.

key_events.event: The opposition held sustained rallies and motorcades demanding Maria Corina Machado's safe return and a presidential election timetable.
A Caracas energy summit brought executives from Eni, Repsol, Qatar, GeoPark, Glencore, and Peabody to discuss gas, diluent, coal, and new fields.
Senate Democrats challenged the Pentagon's proposed equity stake in Venezuelan oil following David Rivera's sentencing.
Power outages and the 100-day earthquake anniversary triggered street protests and renewed housing-compensation demands.

naive_forecast.summary: The naive reading takes the text's top-probability scenarios at face value. The dominant story is the government announcing a formal safe-return framework for Machado, with the opposition holding major street actions demanding elections. The energy sector produces at least two new investment announcements following the Caracas summit. The government makes a visible emergency power plan announcement to address outages in oil-producing regions. In Washington, Senate Democrats mount a public challenge to the Pentagon's equity stake in Venezuelan oil. Domestically, the government introduces a formal legislative step toward the anti-hate law, though this is the least certain of the five events. The overall picture is managed openness: Caracas signals deal-readiness and political flexibility while retaining control of the transition's pace. No election is held, no full IMF program launches, and no sudden production surge occurs.

The government's control of the transition is more fragile than the headline case implies.

The combined power-and-Machado mobilization (35%) is a scenario the text mentions but the naive reading treats as background. The IMF office (55%) is elevated to a primary checkable event.
